16661-george-selwyn:
E. S. Roscoe and Helen Clergue edited George Selwyn's letters and life in this 1899 volume. The first chapter sets Selwyn, his friends, and his age. Correspondence from 1767 to 1769 follows, on Carlisle, Lady Sarah Bunbury, the Duke of Grafton, Charles Fox, card-playing, Almack's, Newmarket, gambling at the clubs, and elections. Later chapters cover politics and society to 1780.

Selwyn writes as a wit of London society, keen on gossip, gaming, and high life. The letters give Georgian England in its own voice. Readers of eighteenth-century letters will find a sparkling, sometimes sharp portrait of a world of clubs, cards, and Parliament.
17402-the-adventures-of-kathlyn:
Harold MacGrath, author of The Man on the Box and The Goose Girl, published this adventure novel in Indianapolis in 1914 with the Bobbs-Merrill Company, dedicating it to W. N. Selig. A frontispiece warns that it will be a hard trek. The chapters promise a golden girl, an unwelcome throne, two ordeals, the court of the lion, a temple, quicksands, and a slave mart.

Later chapters add a colonel in chains and further trials for Kathlyn, the heroine at the centre of the tale. Readers get a popular exotic adventure of the 1910s, in MacGrath's brisk, romantic style, written when the story was also finding a life on screen. It suits readers who enjoy old-fashioned thrills in far places.
3004-jefferson-and-his-colleagues-a-chro:
Allen Johnson wrote Jefferson and His Colleagues, a chronicle of the Virginia dynasty, for the Chronicles of America series. Chapters follow Jefferson's court, the republican tack, and Mediterranean corsairs. The shadow of the first consul, pursuit of the Floridas, an American Catiline, the pacifists of 1807, the war hawks, Madison under fire, and the peacemakers follow. The dynasty runs from Jefferson through Madison. Johnson treats Aaron Burr's western enterprise with care, noting that Burr surely recognized the temper of westerners who hated Spain and loved the Union.

A filibustering expedition against Mexico may have been planned, favored by circumstance and a bellicose presidential message. The book gives a readable account of early republic politics, with personality and policy in balance.
3786-the-recollections-of-geoffrey-hamly:
Henry Kingsley tells this long colonial novel through Geoffrey Hamlyn, whose recollections carry a family from England to Australia. The story opens with the courtship of John Thornton, a clerk, and runs from Trafalgar to the peace of 1818, with forgeries, Brighton races, and a farewell sermon on the way. Then comes the exodus, as the party sails for the south and builds a new life on Australian runs.

Major Buckley, George Hawker, and the vicar people the tale, with trout fishing, horse breaking, and Christmas in a warm climate among its pleasures. A domestic scene of darning, tears, and a child in Mary's lap shows Kingsley's warmth for home life amid the colonial bustle. Readers who like emigrant sagas will find a full, generous novel of two worlds and one family.
6013-viola-gwyn:
George Barr McCutcheon opens with a prologue: Kenneth Gwynne was five years old when his father ran away with Rachel Carter, a widow. From that beginning the story grows into shelter for the night, a strange young woman, and the title figure Viola Gwyn herself. She declares she will marry when and where and whom she pleases.

Chapters follow Barry Lapelle, Isaac Stain appearing by night, the landing of the Paul Revere, tempests and Indians, a trial, and a flight. McCutcheon blends frontier adventure with romance and family reckoning. Rachel delivers a message, Lapelle shows his teeth, and old wrongs press toward judgment.
8165-the-geste-of-duke-jocelyn:
Jeffery Farnol published The Geste of Duke Jocelyn in September 1920 with Little, Brown, with colour illustrations by Eric Pape, though this edition omits them. The book opens with a verse dedication to his daughter Gillian, a child becoming a woman, who already rules her father with an imperious sway, particularly over his socks and ties. The geste itself, a tale of deeds, follows Duke Jocelyn through romance and adventure in Farnol's high-spirited manner.

Farnol was a best-selling romancer, and this book shows his gift for gallant heroes, lively dialogue, and old-world colour. It suits readers who enjoy historical romance without irony, told with warmth and pace. As a period piece of popular fiction, it preserves the charm that made Farnol a household name.
britannica-1911-baird-henry-martyn:
Baird, Henry Martyn (1832-1906), was an American historian and teacher. He was born in Philadelphia in 1832. His father Robert was a Presbyterian preacher. The father worked hard for temperance. The boy spent eight early years in Paris and Geneva.

Baird graduated at New York University in 1850. He then lived two years in Italy and Greece. He studied theology at Union and Princeton seminaries. From 1859 he taught Greek at New York University. He held that chair until his death. His fame rests on Huguenot history. His three great works tell that story in parts. They cover the rise of the Huguenots first. Henry of Navarre follows. The revocation of the Edict of Nantes closes the set. Care, fairness, and high scholarship mark them all.
britannica-1911-brodhead-john-romeyn:
John Romeyn Brodhead (1814–1873) was an American historical scholar born in Philadelphia on 2 January 1814, son of a prominent Dutch Reformed clergyman. He graduated at Rutgers College in 1831 and joined the New York bar in 1835. From 1837 he gave himself chiefly to American colonial history, hunting the records of the early Dutch settlements.

An attache post at the American legation at the Hague in 1839 opened the Dutch archives, which proved rich in material on early New York. The state legislature voted funds for gathering transcripts from European archives, and Governor Seward appointed Brodhead in 1841 to do the work. Within several years he had collected some eighty manuscript volumes of transcripts. Much of it was unused by historians before. O'Callaghan and Fernow later edited the set, and the state published it.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-brooklyn:
Brooklyn's diocese takes all Long Island, 1,007 square miles with about 2,000,000 people, 600,000 of them Catholic. Irish, German, and Italian faithful predominate, yet the Gospel sounds weekly in twelve tongues, from Polish and Syrian to Lithuanian and Bohemian. Spanish explorers named it Isle of the Apostles in 1524, and Dutch West India settlement followed in 1636.

Under Dutch rule Catholicism left scarcely a trace, since cemeteries and tombstones were shunned as popish relics. In 1657 Nicholas the Frenchman was fined twelve guilders for refusing, as a Catholic, to pay the Dutch minister's tax. Walloons, Huguenots, and Acadian exiles later settled the island, and militia rolls of 1775 already carry Irish names like Reilly, Shea, Burke, and Sullivan, though their children's fates are unrecorded.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-josse-raveste:
Josse Ravesteyn was a Flemish theologian of Louvain who helped condemn the teachings of Baius. Born about 1506 at Tielt, he studied philosophy at Louvain, graduated fourth in 1525, and taught there while studying theology under Tapper and Hasselius. He led the College of Houterle from 1540 to 1553 and became professor of theology in 1546.

Sent to the Council of Trent in 1551, Ravesteyn wrote memoranda on penance, extreme unction, and the Mass. At the Worms Conference of 1557 he met Canisius and other Catholic debaters. Through his efforts, Baius' doctrines were censured by Salamanca, Alcalá, Paris, and Pope Pius V in 1567. He directed Louvain's hospital nuns until his death in 1570.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-nicolas-gedoy:
French translator Nicolas Gédoyn carried Quintilian and Pausanias into elegant French and argued for fresh methods in schooling. Born at Orléans in 1667, he entered the Jesuits, taught rhetoric at Blois, and left the order through ill health while keeping its friendship.

A canonry at the Sainte-Chapelle and two abbeys freed him to write, and his free rendering of Quintilian won him a seat in the French Academy in 1718. Essays on taste, translation, child-rearing, and Roman courtesy followed, and he died in 1744. His collected essays include a life of Epaminondas and pieces on Roman courtesy and the ancients.
george-selwyn:
George Selwyn was a wit, clubman, and member of Parliament whose letters open a window on London in the late 1700s. E. S. Roscoe and Helen Clergue edited this 1899 volume of his letters and life. A first chapter sets out Selwyn, his friends, and his age. The letters then run year by year, from 1767 on.

Selwyn writes of Charles James Fox, the Earl of Carlisle, card play at Almack's, races at Newmarket, and dinners with the great. Talk of elections, debts, duels, and court news fills the pages. His tone is dry, shrewd, and fond of gossip. For readers of the period, the letters give the feel of an age from inside its clubs, in the words of a man everyone liked to hear.
jefferson-and-his-colleagues-a-chronicle:
Allen Johnson wrote this chronicle of the Virginia dynasty for the Chronicles of America series, covering the presidencies of Jefferson and Madison. It opens on the morning of March 4, 1801, with Jefferson taking his usual low seat at the boarding-house breakfast table on the day of his inauguration. Fifteen chapters carry the story to the end of an era.

The headings map the era's crises in order. Barbary corsairs, the shadow of Napoleon, the pursuit of the Floridas, and Burr as an American Catiline fill Jefferson's terms. Peaceable coercion, the war-hawks, and Madison under fire lead into the War of 1812 and the peacemakers. A bibliographical note closes the volume. Johnson writes narrative history of the old school, scene by scene.
the-adventures-of-kathlyn: Harold MacGrath, author of The Man on the Box, wrote The Adventures of Kathlyn, printed at Indianapolis by the Bobbs-Merrill Company with rights held in 1914 and a warm note to W. N. Selig. Chapters listed run from The Golden Girl and The Unwelcome Throne through The Court of the Lion, Quicksands, The Slave Mart, The White Elephant, and The Seven Leopards.
the-geste-of-duke-jocelyn:
Jeffery Farnol wrote The Geste of Duke Jocelyn as a romance made for his daughter Gillian, printed in 1920 with color pictures by Eric Pape. A verse letter to Gillian opens the book.

Farnol tells his girl he will fill the book with romance from cover to cover, as the old tale-tellers wrote: in prose, blank verse, and rhyme. Gillian, grown too old for fairy tales, had sighed that novels lack love enough. Her father answers with a duke's geste of sighing lovers, quests, and high deeds, framed as a gift that she may one day read to children of her own.
the-recollections-of-geoffrey-hamlyn:
Henry Kingsley dedicates his novel to his father and mother as the fruit of weary years of separation. Contents open with the courtship and marriage of John Thornton and then follow a family in Europe from Trafalgar to the peace of 1818, promising facts not published before.

Later headings bring new faces, a felony the reader helps conceal, George Hawker at a fair, and Major Buckley holding forth on trout fishing, emigration, and Hawker himself. Here only the title pages, dedication, and opening of the contents list are present, so the recollections themselves do not appear.
viola-gwyn: George Barr McCutcheon wrote Viola Gwyn, a novel with a prologue called The Beginning and twenty-nine chapters. Pages present here hold the title page, contents, and the prologue's heading only, so the story itself is not shown. Chapter titles sketch a frontier tale. They name shelter for the night, a strange young woman, and Barry Lapelle. Later titles promise the landing of the boat Paul Revere, tempests and Indians, and a fight at Hawk's cabin. A flight and the trial of Moll Hawk close the list.
